## Course Description

The goal of this 1 credit course is to provide graduate students in bioengineering and biosciences with foundational understanding of modern computational tools to aid in their research. The target audience is graduate students who have little or no experience with computational tools, or who would like a refresher and exposure to a broad quiver of resources. Learning outcomes for the course are understanding the fundamental aspects of computer systems, including file types, storage structure, and the logic of programming languages. Unix command line for the manipulation of large data sets and running scripts both locally and on UO’s supercomputer Talapas. How to properly organize and format primary data and metadata files for analysis. The use of integrated developer environment (IDE) to write basic scripts in Python and R. NIH’s FAIR (findable, accessible, interoperable and reusable) principle and best practices for reproducible science including the use of Git/GitHub, Markdown and remote databases.

## Course Structure

We will hold class on Mondays from 4:00 to 5:00PM in KC2 213 (September 28 - November 30, 2026), preceded by a kick-off bootcamp on Thursday, September 24 from 9:00AM to 1:00PM in the KC2 Seminar Room. These meetings will be relatively informal, and will usually begin with a 30-45 min. conceptual overview of topics with coding demonstrations. I will post all lecture slides as Markdown and HTML after class to the course website under the 'Lectures' tab. The online [course book](book/index.html), linked above, is the required reading. The [Schedule](Schedule.qmd) and [Lectures](Lectures.qmd) pages list the chapters that go with each week, including the bootcamp. The remaining meeting time will be reserved for group work, questions, answers, and discussion. I encourage students to work on exercises and assignments during these periods so that questions can be directly addressed as they emerge.

## Course Objectives

By the end of the course, students will be able to:

- *Computers and shells* (Weeks 0-3)
  - Describe the fundamental aspects of computer systems - CPUs, GPUs, memory, storage, operating systems and file types - and how local, cluster and cloud computing differ.
  - Navigate a Unix shell (Terminal, or WSL/Ubuntu on Windows) using paths and core commands, and read and write files from the command line.
  - Build data-processing pipelines with standard streams, redirection and pipes, and work with large and compressed genomic data files.
  - Search and filter text with GREP, regular expressions, and related tools such as AWK and SED.
  - Apply the principles of tidy data to properly organize and format primary data and metadata files for analysis.
- *Your computational toolkit* (Bootcamp and throughout)
  - Install and configure R, Python, Quarto, LaTeX (TinyTeX), Git, and an IDE (VS Code or Positron; RStudio optional).
  - Use an IDE to write, run and debug code, and know where UO resources, data protection policies and backups fit in.
- *Foundations of scripting* (Weeks 4-7)
  - Write shell scripts with variables, conditionals, loops and functions, including basic error handling.
  - Read and write code in R and Python, side by side: packages, objects, vectors, data frames and functions.
  - Wrangle and summarize data frames with the tidyverse (R) and pandas (Python), and write your own functions.
  - Create clear, publication-quality figures from data frames (e.g., with ggplot2).
- *High performance computing* (Week 8)
  - Connect to UO's supercomputer cluster, Talapas, via `ssh` and Open OnDemand, and load software modules.
  - Write and submit Slurm scripts for big jobs, monitor them, and understand the basics of parallel computing.
- *Reproducible science* (Weeks 9-10)
  - Articulate the importance of reproducible research and the NIH FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) principles.
  - Write documents in Markdown and Quarto for manuscripts, presentations and websites, including LaTeX mathematical expressions.
  - Use generative AI assistants and 'vibe coding' responsibly, and recognize their misuse.
  - Use Git and GitHub for version control, project management, collaboration and GitHub Pages websites.

## Graded Assignments

**Problem sets:** Students will be assigned two problem sets to complete independently. These will mostly focus on one or a few data sets each, and the goal will be for the students to organize, visualize, analyze, and interpret the data sets in light of specific scientific motivations - 60% of grade.

**Term project:** Students will choose a large dataset to process on Talapas. The goal of this project is allow students agency in applying what they are learning in class to their own data - 40% of grade.

**Preparing and submitting assignments:** The information required to complete all in-class assignments and problem sets will be given in instructions on Canvas. Students should carefully follow the detailed instructions associated with each assignment. Students are encouraged to work together and share information. In particular, some students will have a higher skill level than others, and we encourage those students with more experience to help their peers. *However, no direct sharing of code is allowed.*

**Preparing and submitting assignments:** Assignments will be submitted on Canvas. Be sure to include your name on the document. Be professional – appropriately name your files, make sure they are organized, and submit only the information requested. Late assignments will not be accepted.
